title: Mechanism of eukaryotic origin unwinding is a dual helicase DNA shearing process

venue.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

abstract: DNA replication in all cells begins with the melting of base pairs at the duplex origin to allow access to single-stranded DNA templates which are replicated by DNA polymerases. In bacteria, origin DNA is presumed to be melted by accessory proteins that allow loading of two ring-shaped replicative helicases around single-strand DNA (ssDNA) for bidirectional unwinding and DNA replication. In eukaryotes, by contrast, two replicative CMG (Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS) helicases are initially loaded head to head around origin double-strand DNA (dsDNA), and there does not appear to be a separate origin unwinding factor. This led us to investigate whether head-to-head CMGs use their adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-driven motors to initiate duplex DNA unwinding at the origin. Here, we show that CMG tracks on one strand of the duplex while surrounding it, and this feature allows two head-to-head CMGs to unwind dsDNA by using their respective motors to pull on opposite strands of the duplex. We further show that while CMG is capable of limited duplex unwinding on its own, the extent of unwinding is greatly and rapidly stimulated by addition of the multifunctional CMG-binding protein Mcm10 that is critical for productive initiation of DNA replication in vivo. On the basis of these findings, we propose that Mcm10 is a processivity or positioning factor that helps translate the work performed by the dual CMG motors at the origin into productive unwinding that facilitates bidirectional DNA replication.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, this 2023 article has already drawn measurable scholarly attention, with 12 OpenAlex citations and 13 documented downstream reuse events. Its citation footprint is broad enough to suggest that the paper’s model of eukaryotic origin unwinding is being taken up in ongoing work on DNA replication and helicase function.

Full narrative

Langston, Georgescu, and O’Donnell’s study addresses a central question in DNA replication: how eukaryotic origins are opened to expose single-stranded templates. The paper’s contribution is mechanistically specific and timely, proposing dual-helicase DNA shearing as the basis of origin unwinding in eukaryotes. That framing aligns closely with the article’s core concepts in helicase activity, processivity, and eukaryotic DNA replication, and it places the work squarely in a highly active area of replication biology.

The scholarly record shows that the article is being used beyond a single niche. Citations have accrued steadily since publication, with most appearing in 2024 and additional citations in 2025 and 2026. The citing literature spans research articles, preprints, and a review, and includes venues such as The EMBO Journal, Nature Structural & Molecular Biology, Biochemical Society Transactions, and Current Opinion in Structural Biology. That pattern suggests the paper is serving as a reference point for both primary experiments and synthesis articles on replication initiation.

The downstream reuse signal reinforces that interpretation. The record shows 13 reuse events, including articles, preprints, a review, and an article mention in Europe PMC. Recent citing works focus on closely related questions, such as Mcm10’s role in bracing converging replicative helicases, MCM5 regulation, and broader discussions of genome replication initiation. In other words, the article appears to be helping shape an active mechanistic conversation rather than remaining a standalone finding.

The work also sits within a well-supported research program. The authors are from Rockefeller University, and the paper acknowledges funding from the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the National Institutes of Health, including NIGMS support. Public-discourse signals in the available record are minimal, so the clearest evidence of impact comes from scholarly reuse and citation rather than media or social attention. Overall, the article’s early impact is strongest in the research literature, where it is being cited and reused in exactly the domain it was designed to inform.
